Illustration: Quartz
A magnitude 9.0 earthquake releases roughly 32 times more energy than a magnitude 8.0, and about 1,000 times more than a 7.0. That logarithmic math is why the small group of ruptures above magnitude 8.5 sits in a category of its own. The thousands of other damaging earthquakes logged since seismic networks began keeping score do not come close. The gap between an 8.5 and a 9.5 is not a matter of degree. It is a difference in the physical size of the fault that broke, the length of time the ground moved and the volume of seawater displaced.
The strongest earthquakes in recorded history were not always the deadliest. Death tolls depend on population density, construction standards, the time of day and whether the rupture pushed up a tsunami. A magnitude 8.7 in an uninhabited stretch of the North Pacific can pass with no confirmed fatalities. A far weaker quake beneath a crowded city can kill tens of thousands. Raw energy release and human loss are two separate measurements, and they rarely line up.
This list covers the instrumental era, generally from 1900 onward, because that is when seismic networks became capable of assigning reliable numbers. Earthquakes described in older historical records may have matched or exceeded these, but without seismographs there is no way to measure them. The magnitudes here come from the moment magnitude scale, which replaced the Richter scale for large events. It calculates energy release from the physical dimensions of the fault rupture and the amount of slip, rather than from shaking recorded at a single station.
One pattern runs through nearly every entry. These ruptures occurred along subduction zones, where one tectonic plate grinds beneath another. The boundary locks in place for decades or centuries, then releases the stored strain in a few minutes. Chile, Alaska, Sumatra, Japan and Kamchatka appear repeatedly for that reason. Knowing which boundaries have produced earthquakes this size is the clearest guide to where comparable events remain possible.

## The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile remains the strongest ever recorded
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.5 earthquake that struck near Valdivia in southern Chile on May 22, 1960, is the most powerful earthquake ever measured by seismic instruments. No recorded event since has matched its energy release.
The rupture tore along the Peru-Chile Trench for a stretch estimated at more than 500 miles, as the Nazca Plate slipped beneath the South American Plate. A fault break of that length is what separates the event from everything below it on the scale. Magnitude depends on rupture area and the amount of slip, and few plate boundaries on Earth hold enough continuous locked fault to produce a break this long.
The rupture pushed a tsunami across the entire Pacific basin. Waves struck the Chilean coast within minutes, then crossed deep water at roughly 500 miles per hour toward Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. The first destructive waves reached Hilo, Hawaii, about 15 hours later, more than 6,000 miles from the source, and wrecked much of the downtown waterfront. Hilo rebuilt with open parkland along the bayfront instead of commercial blocks.
Casualty figures for the combined earthquake and tsunami vary by source, ranging from about 1,000 to as high as 6,000. The spread reflects how hard it was to count the dead in 1960. Communications were cut across a sparsely settled, heavily damaged stretch of south-central Chile, and some coastal villages were erased outright. Economic losses were severe, with housing, farmland, ports and rail links destroyed across several provinces.
Valdivia remains the benchmark against which every other large earthquake is measured, and it also sets a practical ceiling in seismic hazard modeling. Anything substantially larger would require a locked fault segment longer than any subduction zone known to store strain. That constraint is why 9.5 is often treated as close to the physical limit of crustal rupture.

## The 1964 Alaska earthquake was the second-strongest ever measured
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.2 earthquake that ruptured beneath Prince William Sound on March 27, 1964, is the second-strongest quake ever recorded and the largest measured in North America. It broke along the Aleutian megathrust, where the Pacific Plate is forced beneath the North American Plate. Many accounts call it the Good Friday earthquake, after the day it struck.
Ground motion continued for four to five minutes across parts of south-central Alaska. That is an extreme duration — most large quakes shake for well under a minute. The sustained motion liquefied unstable ground in Anchorage, roughly 75 miles from the epicenter. Landslides carried away whole blocks of housing in the Turnagain Heights neighborhood and collapsed part of the downtown commercial district.
Tsunamis caused most of the deaths. Waves generated by submarine landslides reached Alaskan fishing communities within minutes of the shaking. The ocean-crossing wave arrived at Crescent City on the northern California coast hours later and killed people there. The combined toll is generally put at about 131 — low for a rupture this size, and a consequence of how thinly populated the affected coastline was in 1964.
The earthquake rearranged the land itself. Surveys afterward found stretches of coast and seafloor lifted by more than 30 feet. Other areas dropped far enough to flood shoreline forests, leaving stands of dead trees in salt water. Geologist George Plafker mapped that pattern of uplift and subsidence. His work showed the rupture had occurred on a shallow-dipping thrust fault. That evidence helped confirm how subduction zones generate the largest earthquakes, at a time when plate tectonics was still being worked out.
The event reshaped warning systems and engineering practice. The U.S. opened a tsunami warning center at Palmer, Alaska, in 1967, after the 1964 waves hit nearby coastlines with no alert. Studies of how Anchorage's slopes and structures behaved during prolonged shaking informed later seismic design standards for soil stability and building performance.

## The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake triggered one of history's deadliest tsunamis
Illustration: Quartz
A magnitude 9.1 earthquake ruptured the seafloor off the northwest coast of Sumatra on December 26, 2004, breaking more than 900 miles of fault and generating the deadliest tsunami in recorded history.
The fault that failed marks the boundary where the Indian Plate descends beneath the Burma microplate, part of the Sunda subduction system. The seafloor lifted along that entire length. The movement displaced an enormous column of water, which spread outward across the Indian Ocean in every direction.
Waves struck Indonesia's Aceh province within roughly 20 to 30 minutes, destroying whole coastal districts of Banda Aceh. Sri Lanka, southern India and the Thai resort coast were hit within one to two hours. Hours after that, the waves still carried enough force to kill people on the coasts of Somalia and Tanzania, thousands of miles from the epicenter.
The death toll is generally placed at about 230,000 people across 14 countries, with Indonesia accounting for the largest share by far. That figure remains an estimate rather than a count. Many victims were never recovered, and some affected communities had no complete population records to measure the loss against.
Wave height alone does not explain the scale of the disaster. The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning network comparable to the system already running in the Pacific. Seismologists registered the earthquake quickly, but no mechanism existed to turn that detection into warnings for the coastal populations in the path of the water. Most people standing on the beaches did not know what the sudden retreat of the sea meant.
The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System was built in the aftermath, connecting seismic sensors, deep-ocean pressure gauges and national alert channels across the region.
The rupture also shifted enough of Earth's mass to shorten the length of a day by a fraction of a microsecond, according to analyses by geophysicists who modeled the event's seismic data.

The number of people dying in natural disasters is lower today than it was in the past; the world has become more resilient.
Earthquakes, however, can still claim a large number of lives. Whilst historically, floods, droughts, and epidemics dominated disaster deaths, a high annual death toll in recent years often results from a major earthquake and possibly a tsunami caused by them. Since 2000, the two peak years in annual death tolls (reaching hundreds of thousands) were 2004 and 2010. Earthquake deaths accounted for 93 percent and 69 percent of disaster deaths, respectively. Both events (the Sumatra earthquake and tsunami of 2004 and the Port-au-Prince earthquake in 2010) are in the deadliest earthquake rankings below.
What have been the most deadly earthquakes in human history? In the visualization, we have mapped the top 10 rankings of known earthquakes, which resulted in the largest number of deaths.1 This ranking is based on mortality estimates from the NOAA's National Geophysical Data Center (NGDC).2
Clicking on the visualization will open it in higher resolution. This ranking is also summarized in table form.
The most deadly earthquake in history was in Shaanxi, China in 1556. It's estimated to have killed 830,000 people. This is more than twice that of the second most fatal: the recent Port-au-Prince earthquake in Haiti in 2010. It's reported that 316,000 people died as a result.3
Two very recent earthquakes— the Sumatra earthquake and tsunami of 2004 and the 2010 Port-au-Prince earthquake — feature amongst the most deadly in human history. But equally, some of the most fatal occurred in the very distant past. The third deadliest was the earthquake in Antakya (Turkey) in 115 CE. Both old and very recent earthquakes feature near the top of the list. The deadly nature of earthquakes has been a persistent threat throughout our history.

| 4 | Antakya, Turkey | 525 | 250,000 | 7 | Severe damage to the area of the Byzantine Empire. The earthquake caused severe damage to many buildings. However, severe damage was also caused by fires in the aftermath combined with strong wind. |  
| 5 | Tangshan, China | 1976 | 242,769 | 7.5 | Reported that the earthquake risk had been greatly underestimated meaning almost all buildings and structures were designed and built without seismic considerations. Estimated that up to 85% of buildings collapsed. Tangshan therefore large comprised of unreinforced brick buildings which resulted in a large death toll. |

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 1. Valdivia, Chile 22 May 1960 (magnitude 9.5)
This earthquake killed 1655 people, injured 3000 and displaced two million. It caused US$550 million damage in Chile, while the tsunami that it spawned caused deaths and damage as far away as Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. The 'rupture zone' of the quake was more than 1000 km long. Two days after the initial quake, the nearby volcano Puyehue erupted, sending ash and steam up to 6 km into the atmosphere over a period of several weeks.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 2. Prince William Sound, Alaska 28 March 1964 (magnitude 9.2)
Compared to the Chilean earthquake, this earthquake was less damaging: the resulting tsunami took 128 lives and caused overall US$311 million in damage. The earthquake was felt mainly over Alaska, as well as some places in Canada, while the tsunami created by it caused damage as far away as Hawaii. The most damage was sustained by the city of Anchorage, 120 km north-west of the epicentre. Shaking from the quake itself is reported to have lasted for three minutes.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 3. Sumatra, Indonesia 26 December 2004 (magnitude 9.1)
In terms of damage and loss of life, the scale of the disaster caused by the resulting Boxing Day Tsunami was enormous. In total, 227,900 people were killed or presumed dead, with around 1.7 million displaced over 14 countries in South Asia and East Africa. The epicentre was 250 km south-east of Band Aceh, Indonesia, at a depth of 30 km. Several days later on 28 December, a mud volcano began erupting near Baratang, Andamar Islands, which is thought to have been associated with the earthquake.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 4. Sendai, Japan 11 March 2011 (magnitude 9.0)
So far the official death toll stands at several thousand from the combined effect of the powerful earthquake, aftershocks and the tsunami. However, the total is expected to rise, with some estimates of a final toll of over 10,000. Economic impacts are expected to be huge, with the shutting down of nuclear reactors which many industries rely on for power.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 5. Kamchatka, Russia 4 November 1952 (magnitude 9.0)
This earthquake generated a tsunami that caused widespread damage in the Hawaiian Islands. Property damage was estimated at around US$1,000,000. Some reports describe waves of over 9 m high at Kaena Point, Oahu. A farmer on Oahu reported the loss of six cows to the tsunami, but no people were reported killed.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 6. Bio-bio, Chile 27 February 2010 (magnitude 8.8)
This earthquake and subsequent tsunami killed at least 521 people, with 56 missing and 12,000 injured. More than 800,000 people were displaced with a total of 1.8m people affected across Chile, where damage was estimated at US$30 billion. The epicentre was 335 km south-west of Santiago, at a depth of 35 km. A minor tsunami travelled across the Pacific causing damage to boats as far away as San Diego, California.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 7. Off the coast of Ecuador 31 January 1906 (magnitude 8.8)
This earthquake caused a tsunami that is reported to have killed between 500 and 1,500 in Ecuador and Colombia. The tsunami travelled as far north as San Francisco, on the west coast of the US, and west to Hawaii and Japan. The tsunami took roughly 12 hours to cross the Pacific to Hilo, Hawaii.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 8. Rat Islands, Alaska 2 April 1965 (magnitude 8.7)
The worst of the damage attributed to this earthquake was caused by a tsunami, reported to be about 10 m high on Shemya Island. The wave caused flooding on Amchitka Island, causing US$10,000 in property damage. No deaths or injuries were reported.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 9. Sumatra, Indonesia 28 March 2005 (magnitude 8.6)
This earthquake killed 1313, with over 400 people injured by the tsunami as far away as Sri Lanka. The epicentre was 205 km north-west of Sibolga, Sumatra, at a depth of 30 km. This region, also the site of the 2004 Boxing Day Tsunami, is particularly geologically active, with three of the 15 biggest known earthquakes having happened here.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 10. Assam - Tibet 15 August 1950 (magnitude 8.6)
This inland earthquake caused widespread damages to buildings as well as large landslides. 780 people were killed in eastern Tibet, with many villages and towns affected across Assam, China, Tibet and India. Oscillations to lake levels occurred as far away as Norway. The total death toll is likely to be higher, as no definitive total was ever estimated. While the earthquake itself is known as the Assam Earthquake, it is believed the epicentre may have been in Tibet.

Earthquakes described in older historical records may have matched or exceeded these, but without seismographs there is no way to measure them. The magnitudes here come from the moment magnitude scale, which replaced the Richter scale for large events. It calculates energy release from the physical dimensions of the fault rupture and the amount of slip, rather than from shaking recorded at a single station.
One pattern runs through nearly every entry. These ruptures occurred along subduction zones, where one tectonic plate grinds beneath another. The boundary locks in place for decades or centuries, then releases the stored strain in a few minutes. Chile, Alaska, Sumatra, Japan and Kamchatka appear repeatedly for that reason. Knowing which boundaries have produced earthquakes this size is the clearest guide to where comparable events remain possible.

## The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile remains the strongest ever recorded
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.5 earthquake that struck near Valdivia in southern Chile on May 22, 1960, is the most powerful earthquake ever measured by seismic instruments. No recorded event since has matched its energy release.
The rupture tore along the Peru-Chile Trench for a stretch estimated at more than 500 miles, as the Nazca Plate slipped beneath the South American Plate. A fault break of that length is what separates the event from everything below it on the scale. Magnitude depends on rupture area and the amount of slip, and few plate boundaries on Earth hold enough continuous locked fault to produce a break this long.
The rupture pushed a tsunami across the entire Pacific basin. Waves struck the Chilean coast within minutes, then crossed deep water at roughly 500 miles per hour toward Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. The first destructive waves reached Hilo, Hawaii, about 15 hours later, more than 6,000 miles from the source, and wrecked much of the downtown waterfront. Hilo rebuilt with open parkland along the bayfront instead of commercial blocks.
Casualty figures for the combined earthquake and tsunami vary by source, ranging from about 1,000 to as high as 6,000. The spread reflects how hard it was to count the dead in 1960. Communications were cut across a sparsely settled, heavily damaged stretch of south-central Chile, and some coastal villages were erased outright. Economic losses were severe, with housing, farmland, ports and rail links destroyed across several provinces.
Valdivia remains the benchmark against which every other large earthquake is measured, and it also sets a practical ceiling in seismic hazard modeling. Anything substantially larger would require a locked fault segment longer than any subduction zone known to store strain. That constraint is why 9.5 is often treated as close to the physical limit of crustal rupture.

## The 1964 Alaska earthquake was the second-strongest ever measured
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.2 earthquake that ruptured beneath Prince William Sound on March 27, 1964, is the second-strongest quake ever recorded and the largest measured in North America. It broke along the Aleutian megathrust, where the Pacific Plate is forced beneath the North American Plate. Many accounts call it the Good Friday earthquake, after the day it struck.
Ground motion continued for four to five minutes across parts of south-central Alaska. That is an extreme duration — most large quakes shake for well under a minute. The sustained motion liquefied unstable ground in Anchorage, roughly 75 miles from the epicenter. Landslides carried away whole blocks of housing in the Turnagain Heights neighborhood and collapsed part of the downtown commercial district.
Tsunamis caused most of the deaths. Waves generated by submarine landslides reached Alaskan fishing communities within minutes of the shaking. The ocean-crossing wave arrived at Crescent City on the northern California coast hours later and killed people there. The combined toll is generally put at about 131 — low for a rupture this size, and a consequence of how thinly populated the affected coastline was in 1964.
The earthquake rearranged the land itself. Surveys afterward found stretches of coast and seafloor lifted by more than 30 feet. Other areas dropped far enough to flood shoreline forests, leaving stands of dead trees in salt water. Geologist George Plafker mapped that pattern of uplift and subsidence. His work showed the rupture had occurred on a shallow-dipping thrust fault. That evidence helped confirm how subduction zones generate the largest earthquakes, at a time when plate tectonics was still being worked out.
The event reshaped warning systems and engineering practice. The U.S. opened a tsunami warning center at Palmer, Alaska, in 1967, after the 1964 waves hit nearby coastlines with no alert. Studies of how Anchorage's slopes and structures behaved during prolonged shaking informed later seismic design standards for soil stability and building performance.

## The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake triggered one of history's deadliest tsunamis
Illustration: Quartz
A magnitude 9.1 earthquake ruptured the seafloor off the northwest coast of Sumatra on December 26, 2004, breaking more than 900 miles of fault and generating the deadliest tsunami in recorded history.
The fault that failed marks the boundary where the Indian Plate descends beneath the Burma microplate, part of the Sunda subduction system. The seafloor lifted along that entire length. The movement displaced an enormous column of water, which spread outward across the Indian Ocean in every direction.
Waves struck Indonesia's Aceh province within roughly 20 to 30 minutes, destroying whole coastal districts of Banda Aceh. Sri Lanka, southern India and the Thai resort coast were hit within one to two hours. Hours after that, the waves still carried enough force to kill people on the coasts of Somalia and Tanzania, thousands of miles from the epicenter.
The death toll is generally placed at about 230,000 people across 14 countries, with Indonesia accounting for the largest share by far. That figure remains an estimate rather than a count. Many victims were never recovered, and some affected communities had no complete population records to measure the loss against.
Wave height alone does not explain the scale of the disaster. The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning network comparable to the system already running in the Pacific. Seismologists registered the earthquake quickly, but no mechanism existed to turn that detection into warnings for the coastal populations in the path of the water. Most people standing on the beaches did not know what the sudden retreat of the sea meant.
The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System was built in the aftermath, connecting seismic sensors, deep-ocean pressure gauges and national alert channels across the region.
The rupture also shifted enough of Earth's mass to shorten the length of a day by a fraction of a microsecond, according to analyses by geophysicists who modeled the event's seismic data.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 1. Valdivia, Chile 22 May 1960 (magnitude 9.5)
This earthquake killed 1655 people, injured 3000 and displaced two million. It caused US$550 million damage in Chile, while the tsunami that it spawned caused deaths and damage as far away as Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. The 'rupture zone' of the quake was more than 1000 km long. Two days after the initial quake, the nearby volcano Puyehue erupted, sending ash and steam up to 6 km into the atmosphere over a period of several weeks.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 2. Prince William Sound, Alaska 28 March 1964 (magnitude 9.2)
Compared to the Chilean earthquake, this earthquake was less damaging: the resulting tsunami took 128 lives and caused overall US$311 million in damage. The earthquake was felt mainly over Alaska, as well as some places in Canada, while the tsunami created by it caused damage as far away as Hawaii. The most damage was sustained by the city of Anchorage, 120 km north-west of the epicentre. Shaking from the quake itself is reported to have lasted for three minutes.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 3. Sumatra, Indonesia 26 December 2004 (magnitude 9.1)
In terms of damage and loss of life, the scale of the disaster caused by the resulting Boxing Day Tsunami was enormous. In total, 227,900 people were killed or presumed dead, with around 1.7 million displaced over 14 countries in South Asia and East Africa. The epicentre was 250 km south-east of Band Aceh, Indonesia, at a depth of 30 km. Several days later on 28 December, a mud volcano began erupting near Baratang, Andamar Islands, which is thought to have been associated with the earthquake.

### 4. Sendai, Japan 11 March 2011 (magnitude 9.0)
So far the official death toll stands at several thousand from the combined effect of the powerful earthquake, aftershocks and the tsunami. However, the total is expected to rise, with some estimates of a final toll of over 10,000. Economic impacts are expected to be huge, with the shutting down of nuclear reactors which many industries rely on for power.

### 10. Assam - Tibet 15 August 1950 (magnitude 8.6)

The number of people dying in natural disasters is lower today than it was in the past; the world has become more resilient.
Earthquakes, however, can still claim a large number of lives. Whilst historically, floods, droughts, and epidemics dominated disaster deaths, a high annual death toll in recent years often results from a major earthquake and possibly a tsunami caused by them. Since 2000, the two peak years in annual death tolls (reaching hundreds of thousands) were 2004 and 2010. Earthquake deaths accounted for 93 percent and 69 percent of disaster deaths, respectively. Both events (the Sumatra earthquake and tsunami of 2004 and the Port-au-Prince earthquake in 2010) are in the deadliest earthquake rankings below.
What have been the most deadly earthquakes in human history? In the visualization, we have mapped the top 10 rankings of known earthquakes, which resulted in the largest number of deaths.1 This ranking is based on mortality estimates from the NOAA's National Geophysical Data Center (NGDC).2
Clicking on the visualization will open it in higher resolution. This ranking is also summarized in table form.
The most deadly earthquake in history was in Shaanxi, China in 1556. It's estimated to have killed 830,000 people. This is more than twice that of the second most fatal: the recent Port-au-Prince earthquake in Haiti in 2010. It's reported that 316,000 people died as a result.3
Two very recent earthquakes— the Sumatra earthquake and tsunami of 2004 and the 2010 Port-au-Prince earthquake — feature amongst the most deadly in human history. But equally, some of the most fatal occurred in the very distant past. The third deadliest was the earthquake in Antakya (Turkey) in 115 CE. Both old and very recent earthquakes feature near the top of the list. The deadly nature of earthquakes has been a persistent threat throughout our history.

Waves struck the Chilean coast within minutes, then crossed deep water at roughly 500 miles per hour toward Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. The first destructive waves reached Hilo, Hawaii, about 15 hours later, more than 6,000 miles from the source, and wrecked much of the downtown waterfront. Hilo rebuilt with open parkland along the bayfront instead of commercial blocks.
Casualty figures for the combined earthquake and tsunami vary by source, ranging from about 1,000 to as high as 6,000. The spread reflects how hard it was to count the dead in 1960. Communications were cut across a sparsely settled, heavily damaged stretch of south-central Chile, and some coastal villages were erased outright. Economic losses were severe, with housing, farmland, ports and rail links destroyed across several provinces.
Valdivia remains the benchmark against which every other large earthquake is measured, and it also sets a practical ceiling in seismic hazard modeling. Anything substantially larger would require a locked fault segment longer than any subduction zone known to store strain. That constraint is why 9.5 is often treated as close to the physical limit of crustal rupture.

## The 1964 Alaska earthquake was the second-strongest ever measured
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.2 earthquake that ruptured beneath Prince William Sound on March 27, 1964, is the second-strongest quake ever recorded and the largest measured in North America. It broke along the Aleutian megathrust, where the Pacific Plate is forced beneath the North American Plate. Many accounts call it the Good Friday earthquake, after the day it struck.
Ground motion continued for four to five minutes across parts of south-central Alaska. That is an extreme duration — most large quakes shake for well under a minute. The sustained motion liquefied unstable ground in Anchorage, roughly 75 miles from the epicenter. Landslides carried away whole blocks of housing in the Turnagain Heights neighborhood and collapsed part of the downtown commercial district.
Tsunamis caused most of the deaths. Waves generated by submarine landslides reached Alaskan fishing communities within minutes of the shaking. The ocean-crossing wave arrived at Crescent City on the northern California coast hours later and killed people there. The combined toll is generally put at about 131 — low for a rupture this size, and a consequence of how thinly populated the affected coastline was in 1964.
The earthquake rearranged the land itself. Surveys afterward found stretches of coast and seafloor lifted by more than 30 feet. Other areas dropped far enough to flood shoreline forests, leaving stands of dead trees in salt water. Geologist George Plafker mapped that pattern of uplift and subsidence. His work showed the rupture had occurred on a shallow-dipping thrust fault. That evidence helped confirm how subduction zones generate the largest earthquakes, at a time when plate tectonics was still being worked out.
The event reshaped warning systems and engineering practice. The U.S. opened a tsunami warning center at Palmer, Alaska, in 1967, after the 1964 waves hit nearby coastlines with no alert. Studies of how Anchorage's slopes and structures behaved during prolonged shaking informed later seismic design standards for soil stability and building performance.

## The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake triggered one of history's deadliest tsunamis
Illustration: Quartz
A magnitude 9.1 earthquake ruptured the seafloor off the northwest coast of Sumatra on December 26, 2004, breaking more than 900 miles of fault and generating the deadliest tsunami in recorded history.
The fault that failed marks the boundary where the Indian Plate descends beneath the Burma microplate, part of the Sunda subduction system. The seafloor lifted along that entire length. The movement displaced an enormous column of water, which spread outward across the Indian Ocean in every direction.
Waves struck Indonesia's Aceh province within roughly 20 to 30 minutes, destroying whole coastal districts of Banda Aceh. Sri Lanka, southern India and the Thai resort coast were hit within one to two hours. Hours after that, the waves still carried enough force to kill people on the coasts of Somalia and Tanzania, thousands of miles from the epicenter.
The death toll is generally placed at about 230,000 people across 14 countries, with Indonesia accounting for the largest share by far. That figure remains an estimate rather than a count. Many victims were never recovered, and some affected communities had no complete population records to measure the loss against.
Wave height alone does not explain the scale of the disaster. The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning network comparable to the system already running in the Pacific. Seismologists registered the earthquake quickly, but no mechanism existed to turn that detection into warnings for the coastal populations in the path of the water. Most people standing on the beaches did not know what the sudden retreat of the sea meant.
The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System was built in the aftermath, connecting seismic sensors, deep-ocean pressure gauges and national alert channels across the region.
The rupture also shifted enough of Earth's mass to shorten the length of a day by a fraction of a microsecond, according to analyses by geophysicists who modeled the event's seismic data.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 1. Valdivia, Chile 22 May 1960 (magnitude 9.5)
This earthquake killed 1655 people, injured 3000 and displaced two million. It caused US$550 million damage in Chile, while the tsunami that it spawned caused deaths and damage as far away as Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. The 'rupture zone' of the quake was more than 1000 km long. Two days after the initial quake, the nearby volcano Puyehue erupted, sending ash and steam up to 6 km into the atmosphere over a period of several weeks.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 2. Prince William Sound, Alaska 28 March 1964 (magnitude 9.2)
Compared to the Chilean earthquake, this earthquake was less damaging: the resulting tsunami took 128 lives and caused overall US$311 million in damage. The earthquake was felt mainly over Alaska, as well as some places in Canada, while the tsunami created by it caused damage as far away as Hawaii. The most damage was sustained by the city of Anchorage, 120 km north-west of the epicentre. Shaking from the quake itself is reported to have lasted for three minutes.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 3. Sumatra, Indonesia 26 December 2004 (magnitude 9.1)
In terms of damage and loss of life, the scale of the disaster caused by the resulting Boxing Day Tsunami was enormous. In total, 227,900 people were killed or presumed dead, with around 1.7 million displaced over 14 countries in South Asia and East Africa. The epicentre was 250 km south-east of Band Aceh, Indonesia, at a depth of 30 km. Several days later on 28 December, a mud volcano began erupting near Baratang, Andamar Islands, which is thought to have been associated with the earthquake.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 4. Sendai, Japan 11 March 2011 (magnitude 9.0)
So far the official death toll stands at several thousand from the combined effect of the powerful earthquake, aftershocks and the tsunami. However, the total is expected to rise, with some estimates of a final toll of over 10,000. Economic impacts are expected to be huge, with the shutting down of nuclear reactors which many industries rely on for power.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 5. Kamchatka, Russia 4 November 1952 (magnitude 9.0)
This earthquake generated a tsunami that caused widespread damage in the Hawaiian Islands. Property damage was estimated at around US$1,000,000. Some reports describe waves of over 9 m high at Kaena Point, Oahu. A farmer on Oahu reported the loss of six cows to the tsunami, but no people were reported killed.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 6. Bio-bio, Chile 27 February 2010 (magnitude 8.8)
This earthquake and subsequent tsunami killed at least 521 people, with 56 missing and 12,000 injured. More than 800,000 people were displaced with a total of 1.8m people affected across Chile, where damage was estimated at US$30 billion. The epicentre was 335 km south-west of Santiago, at a depth of 35 km. A minor tsunami travelled across the Pacific causing damage to boats as far away as San Diego, California.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 7. Off the coast of Ecuador 31 January 1906 (magnitude 8.8)
This earthquake caused a tsunami that is reported to have killed between 500 and 1,500 in Ecuador and Colombia. The tsunami travelled as far north as San Francisco, on the west coast of the US, and west to Hawaii and Japan. The tsunami took roughly 12 hours to cross the Pacific to Hilo, Hawaii.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 8. Rat Islands, Alaska 2 April 1965 (magnitude 8.7)
The worst of the damage attributed to this earthquake was caused by a tsunami, reported to be about 10 m high on Shemya Island. The wave caused flooding on Amchitka Island, causing US$10,000 in property damage. No deaths or injuries were reported.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 9. Sumatra, Indonesia 28 March 2005 (magnitude 8.6)
This earthquake killed 1313, with over 400 people injured by the tsunami as far away as Sri Lanka. The epicentre was 205 km north-west of Sibolga, Sumatra, at a depth of 30 km. This region, also the site of the 2004 Boxing Day Tsunami, is particularly geologically active, with three of the 15 biggest known earthquakes having happened here.

## The 10 largest magnitudes in recorded history
### 10. Assam - Tibet 15 August 1950 (magnitude 8.6)
This inland earthquake caused widespread damages to buildings as well as large landslides. 780 people were killed in eastern Tibet, with many villages and towns affected across Assam, China, Tibet and India. Oscillations to lake levels occurred as far away as Norway. The total death toll is likely to be higher, as no definitive total was ever estimated. While the earthquake itself is known as the Assam Earthquake, it is believed the epicentre may have been in Tibet.

Title: What were the world's deadliest earthquakes?

The number of people dying in natural disasters is lower today than it was in the past; the world has become more resilient.
Earthquakes, however, can still claim a large number of lives. Whilst historically, floods, droughts, and epidemics dominated disaster deaths, a high annual death toll in recent years often results from a major earthquake and possibly a tsunami caused by them. Since 2000, the two peak years in annual death tolls (reaching hundreds of thousands) were 2004 and 2010. Earthquake deaths accounted for 93 percent and 69 percent of disaster deaths, respectively. Both events (the Sumatra earthquake and tsunami of 2004 and the Port-au-Prince earthquake in 2010) are in the deadliest earthquake rankings below.
What have been the most deadly earthquakes in human history? In the visualization, we have mapped the top 10 rankings of known earthquakes, which resulted in the largest number of deaths.1 This ranking is based on mortality estimates from the NOAA's National Geophysical Data Center (NGDC).2
Clicking on the visualization will open it in higher resolution. This ranking is also summarized in table form.
The most deadly earthquake in history was in Shaanxi, China in 1556. It's estimated to have killed 830,000 people. This is more than twice that of the second most fatal: the recent Port-au-Prince earthquake in Haiti in 2010. It's reported that 316,000 people died as a result.3
Two very recent earthquakes— the Sumatra earthquake and tsunami of 2004 and the 2010 Port-au-Prince earthquake — feature amongst the most deadly in human history. But equally, some of the most fatal occurred in the very distant past. The third deadliest was the earthquake in Antakya (Turkey) in 115 CE. Both old and very recent earthquakes feature near the top of the list. The deadly nature of earthquakes has been a persistent threat throughout our history.
